title: Hardware Helix: Node Rehab and Staged Capacity Onramp
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a procedural draft for 'node rehab' — the end-to-end activities to reintroduce a physical compute node (or set of nodes) after a partial accelerator failure, hardware replacement, or maintenance window. The emphasis is on staged capacity onramp to avoid cache-warm spikes, token backlog storms, and negative tail-latency impacts for production workloads. This is intended for SREs on-call and the hardware ops team.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to nodes in the production serving clusters that host GPU-backed inference pods.
- Node may have had: single-GPU replacement (cartridge/swappable), NVMe reseat, PCIe cable replacement, or firmware update.
- Control plane (k8s, routing, autoscaler) is functioning. If control plane is degraded, escalate per 'cluster-controlplane-failure' runbook instead.
- We assume access to out-of-band console (iDRAC/iLO), SSH jumpboxes, and hardware inventory system.

High-level goals:
1) Restore node to healthy state with minimal customer-impact.
2) Ramp capacity in measured stages to restore throughput and maintain latency SLOs.
3) Record actions and timing for post-incident review.

Preflight checklist (before powering a repaired node back into service):
- Confirm firmware and driver versions match the cluster baseline: nvidia-smi reports expected driver (e.g., 525.x) and CUDA toolkit ABI consistent.
- Validate BIOS and BMC firmware applied and recorded in inventory.
- NVMe health: run smartctl on boot device shows no pending media or reallocated sectors.
- PCIe topology: lspci output indicates expected accelerator present and not in unknown state.
- Security: KMS/HSM agent present and able to access node keys.
- Monitoring: node exports metrics to prometheus (node exporter, dcgm-exporter) and logs appear in logging pipeline.
- Capacity flag: mark node as 'rehab-ready' in the fleet inventory so automation pipelines can target it.

Step-by-step rehab and staged onramp (operational):
1) Soft-attach to control plane (maintenance mode):
   - Add a taint: kubectl taint node <node> rehab=true:NoSchedule --overwrite  # prevents new pods while we validate
   - Delete any leftover inference pods if in a bad state: kubectl delete pod -n redwood-inference --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> --force --grace-period=0

2) Validate runtime stack (on node):
   - Check GPU dir and device nodes: ls -l /dev/nvidia*
   - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv\
   - dcgmi diagnostics (or dcgm-exporter smoke test) to ensure NVML returns expected telemetry.
   - Start a canary container with the same gdk/driver stack: docker run --gpus all --rm nvidia/cuda:12.1-base nvidia-smi
   - Verify nv_peer_mem if used for multi-GPU communication (for PCIe fabric nodes).

3) Local functional tests (no traffic to downstream services):
   - Run a short inference sanity test using a pinned lightweight model: /opt/tools/infer-smoke --model small-serve --batch 1 --seq 64 --duration 30s\
   - Verify no OOMs, no GPU kernel hangs, and stable GPU temperature (no thermal throttling).
   - Run NVMe read/write micro-benchmark to ensure storage latency ok for model cache.

4) Leak and metric observation window (10-15 minutes):
   - Set node to 'quarantine' routing weight=0 but allow load test from canary harness.
   - Watch p95/p99 CPU and GPU utilization, per-process memory, and GPU ECC counters for anomalies.
   - Ensure prometheus metrics for node appear and traces flow to observability.

5) Staged capacity onramp (gradual return to production):
   - Stage A (10% of node capacity): Uncordon with a local scheduling limit via admission: label node rehab-stage=A and apply scheduler annotation to accept small pods only. Use k8s nodeSelector or pod affinity limits for canary routes. Duration: 5-10 minutes.
   - Stage B (40%): If Stage A stable, increase allowed pods and enable a low-traffic subset of routes (non-priority customer routes). Duration: 10-20 minutes.
   - Stage C (80-100%): If Stage B stable, remove rehab taint and lift scheduler caps. Let autoscaler place production pods and monitor for 30 minutes.
Notes on traffic shaping: we use routing policy 'rehab' in gateway config to steer only low-priority traffic during early stages. See linked artifact confluence:INFR-helix-rehab-v1 for route naming.

Automated commands and small scripts (examples):
- Mark node in inventory: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://inventory.internal/api/v1/nodes/<node>/tags -d '{"tags":["rehab-ready"]}'
- Apply taint: kubectl taint node <node> rehab=true:NoSchedule --overwrite
- Quick smoke container: kubectl run smoke-<node> -n infra-test --image=registry.internal/smoke:latest --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeName":"<node>","containers":[{"name":"smoke","image":"registry.internal/smoke:latest","resources":{"limits":{"nvidia.com/gpu":1}}}]}}' -- /bin/sh -c "python smoke.py --model small"

Monitoring checklist during onramp (SLO guardrails):
- p99 latency for inference routes on the node's pods must stay < 2x baseline (defined in console).
- Error rate increase on rehab-route must be < 0.25% absolute.
- GPU ECC errors: none beyond transient single-counters. Any persistent ECC corrections -> halt and escalate.
- OOMKill events: zero allowed.
- Queue depth: no more than 1.5x steady-state for the node group.

Escalation and abort conditions (immediate halt to onramp):
- GPU kernel hang or driver crash observed in dmesg or journald.
- p99 latency > 2x baseline for > 3 consecutive minutes.
- Any under/over-temperature threshold: temperature > 85C sustained or thermal-throttle messages.
- NVMe SMART indicates new critical media errors.
- Pod OOMKills > 0 over a 5 minute window.
If any of the above occur: revert routing (drain node), re-apply rehab taint, notify hardware ops and create an incident ticket with logs attached.

Rollback sequence (safe evacuation):
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=120
- Mark node as 'needs-inspection' in inventory and schedule immediate hardware follow-up.

Post-incident / post-rehab notes to capture (for review):
- Time window: start of rehab -> full onramp completion and exact timestamps for each stage.
- Observed metrics: latency percentiles, GPU utilization, ECC events, NVMe errors, pod restarts. Attach snapshots/links.
- Commands run and any manual fixes performed (firmware flash, reseat, cable change).
- Owner and approver signatures for returning node to production.
- Recommended follow-ups: swap vendor part X, extend thermal monitoring, update inventory record with serial and FRU numbers.

Runbook testing and drills:
- Quarterly tabletop: simulate a single-GPU swap and walk through staged onramp decisions.
- Canary-week: randomly tag 1% of nodes 'rehab-test' and perform non-impacting onramp to validate automation.

Open questions / TODOs (items to finalize in next revision):
- Formalize the exact scheduler annotation keys used for 'Stage A' throttling (currently ad-hoc across clusters).
- Automation: integrate rebuilt-node tagging into infra/telemetry pipeline so taint/uncordon can be triggered by the hardware ops ticketing system.
- Define exact metric thresholds (p99 multipliers) per customer tier (priority vs low-tier).

Appendix: useful commands and locations
- Logs: journalctl -u kubelet -f --since "10m"  # node-level kubelet logs
- GPU logs: dmesg | grep -i nvidia; /var/log/gpu-driver.log
- Inventory API: https://inventory.internal/docs (auth via service token)
- Observability dashboards: Console -> Observability -> Cluster -> NodeGroup -> <node>
